pages.cardBlurb: The site baseline, what changes by trade, and the winter layers that keep a crew on the tools.
pages.h1: Construction workwear: the site baseline and up.
pages.metaTitle: Construction Workwear Guide: Site Kit by Trade | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: What UK construction sites actually require — the hi-vis/boots/head baseline, how kit changes from groundworker to site manager, and layering that survives winter on the tools.
pages.lede: Every UK site starts from the same induction checklist — hi-vis, safety boots, head protection — and then the trade takes over. A groundworker's kit list and a site manager's barely overlap beyond the baseline. Here's the baseline, and what each trade stacks on top.

blocks.h2: What the induction gate checks
blocks.html:
Principal contractors set the entry requirements, and on most UK sites they've converged: hi-vis upper body (Class 2 vest or better — Class 3 near live traffic), S3 safety boots (toe cap, midsole, water-resistant — the codes decoded), and a hard hat. Gloves and eye protection follow the task rather than the gate.

Two things trip people up. First, the site rules are usually stricter than the law — "S3 boots with ankle support" is a contract condition, not an HSE requirement, and arguing the difference at the gate doesn't work. Second, the baseline is a floor: it protects you from the site's general risks, not your trade's specific ones. That's what the rest of the kit list is for.

blocks.h2: What each trade adds to the baseline
blocks.lead: Baseline assumed: Class 2 hi-vis, S3 boots, hard hat.

blocks.h2: Winter is a layering problem, not a jacket problem
blocks.html:
The crews that stay warm on winter sites layer deliberately: a wicking base layer (never cotton against skin — it holds sweat and chills), a fleece or softshell mid-layer, and a certified hi-vis outer. The mistake is a thick non-hi-vis coat zipped over the vest — cover the fluoro and the certification is covered with it. If the outer layer is the warm layer, the outer layer must be the hi-vis layer.

Wet kit is a compliance problem too: a soaked jacket that's stopped beading needs reproofing, and faded hi-vis stops being hi-vis.

blocks.h2: Three decisions that save money later

items.l: S3 across the board, S5 wellingtons for the groundworks gang — not one compromise boot
Coated gloves are consumables; a torn glove replaced beats an injury claimed
Fleet consistency reads as a managed site — and simplifies reordering

blocks.h2: Construction kit FAQ

faq.q: What PPE do you need on a UK construction site?
faq.a: The near-universal induction baseline is hi-vis upper body (Class 2 minimum), S3 safety boots and a hard hat, with gloves and eye protection required task-by-task. Individual principal contractors commonly go further — Class 3 hi-vis, ankle support, mandatory gloves — so the site induction pack is the document that decides.

faq.q: Do all construction workers need Class 3 hi-vis?
faq.a: No — Class 2 is the common site default. Class 3 becomes the requirement around live traffic, plant movements and highways interfaces, and for anyone working in poor light. Many firms simply issue Class 3 jackets for winter since they double as the warm layer.

faq.q: What boots are best for groundworkers?
faq.a: For excavation and concrete work, S5 safety wellingtons — waterproof by construction, with midsole and cleated sole. For general site work between pours, S3 leather boots. Many groundworkers run both and switch by task.

faq.q: Can you wear a normal coat over hi-vis on site?
faq.a: Not while relying on the hi-vis — covering the fluorescent material removes the certified visible area. If the coat is the outer layer, the coat must be the certified hi-vis garment; layer warmth underneath it instead.

pages.cardBlurb: Kit by zone — ambient picking, loading dock, cold store and yard are four different wardrobes.
pages.h1: Warehouse & logistics workwear, zone by zone.
pages.metaTitle: Warehouse & Logistics Workwear Guide: Kit by Zone | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Warehouse kit is a zone problem — what pickers, dock crews, cold-store operatives and yard staff each need, from safety trainers and Class 1 vests to EN 342 coldstore suits.
pages.lede: A distribution centre isn't one environment — it's four. The picker on the mezzanine, the loader on the dock, the operative in the minus-25 chamber and the shunter in the yard are dressed for different jobs, and treating them as one "warehouse kit" is how firms end up with cold pickers and sweating loaders.

heroMeta.l: Cold store is its own world

blocks.lead: Where someone spends their shift decides what they wear — the table is the guide in miniature.

blocks.h2: Trainers beat boots — until they don't
blocks.html:
The biggest comfort win in warehousing this decade is the S1P safety trainer: same certified toe cap and midsole as a boot, a fraction of the weight, and pickers walking 15 km a shift feel every gram. On dry internal floors it's the right call, and fighting it on tradition costs you the workforce's goodwill.

It stops being the right call where water, weather or rough ground enter: open docks, yards, waste areas. That's S3 territory — water-resistant upper, cleated sole. The honest setup for most DCs is trainers inside, boots for the yard-facing roles, and no one-size policy.

blocks.h2: Cold store kit is safety kit, not comfort kit
blocks.html:
At chill temperatures (0–5 °C) lined trousers, a thermal base layer and insulated gloves keep a full shift workable. In a freezer chamber at −18 to −25 °C, clothing is the difference between a safe rotation and cold stress: a one- or two-piece EN 342-rated coldstore suit, insulated CI-rated footwear, lined waterproof gloves and covered ears are the working minimum, with wind-chill from evaporator fans making the effective temperature lower than the dial says.

Two details that get missed: sweat is the enemy — over-dressed workers who sweat then chill are colder than under-dressed ones, which is why suits are sized for a base layer, not a jumper pile; and door transitions — staff moving chamber-to-ambient repeatedly need layers they can vent, or condensation soaks the insulation from inside.

blocks.h2: What logistics employers standardise

items.l: Hi-vis on = anywhere MHE runs; the rule survives because it's simple
Carton-handling gloves are consumables — stock them like tape
EN 342 suits are personal issue; shared suits end up soaked and unworn

blocks.h2: Warehouse kit FAQ

faq.q: What hi-vis class do warehouse workers need?
faq.a: Indoors around forklifts and MHE, Class 1 or 2 is the norm — many operations simply mandate a Class 2 vest everywhere past the door because one simple rule beats zone-by-zone policing. Yard and shunting roles around HGVs step up to Class 3.

faq.q: Are safety trainers OK for warehouse work?
faq.a: Yes — an S1P safety trainer carries the same certified toe cap and midsole as a boot and is the comfortable default for pickers on dry internal floors. Roles that face weather, water or rough ground (docks, yards) should be in S3 boots instead.

faq.q: What do you wear in a cold store?
faq.a: For freezer work at −18 to −25 °C: an EN 342-rated coldstore suit over a wicking base layer, insulated CI-rated safety boots, lined gloves and head covering. At chill temperatures, lined trousers, a thermal base layer and insulated gloves usually carry a shift.

faq.q: Why do cold store workers get too cold even in rated suits?
faq.a: Usually sweat or fit: over-layering under the suit causes sweating, and damp insulation loses its warmth; suits also need sizing that traps an air layer rather than compressing it. Wind-chill from evaporator fans adds a real effect the thermometer doesn't show.

pages.cardBlurb: Coveralls done right, gloves matched to the process, and the line where ordinary kit ends and FR begins.
pages.h1: Manufacturing workwear: coveralls, gloves & the FR line.
pages.metaDesc: Workwear for factories and workshops — why the coverall is still the base layer, matching EN 388 glove levels to the process, and where flame-resistant kit becomes mandatory.
pages.lede: Factory kit has one organising idea: the process dictates the garment. A machine shop, a fabrication bay and an assembly line share a roof but not a kit list — and the fastest way to spec it is to walk the processes, not the job titles.

heroMeta.l: Loose cuffs and machines don't mix

blocks.h2: The coverall survived for a reason
blocks.html:
The coverall remains manufacturing's default because it solves three problems at once: it covers the torso and legs in one garment with no waist gap, it has no loose hem to catch, and it takes industrial laundering. Poly-cotton handles general machining and assembly; heavier cotton drill suits hot, dirty work; and once processes involve flame or arc, the coverall goes FR — a different garment entirely.

Fit rules matter more here than anywhere: cuffs close, zips done, nothing flapping. Rotating machinery turns loose fabric into a winch line — it's why workshop rules ban dangling drawstrings and why coverall cuffs button or elasticate. Two-piece alternatives (work trousers + polo or sweatshirt) suit assembly and inspection roles where the machine risk is lower and comfort wins.

blocks.h2: Match the glove to the process
blocks.lead: One factory, four glove specs — buying a single glove for everyone protects no one properly.
head: Process
Glove
EN 388 spec to look for
rows: EN 407 / EN 12477, not an EN 388 buy

blocks.h2: Where ordinary workwear stops being legal
blocks.html:
The moment a process involves welding, grinding sparks, open flame or electrical arc risk, ordinary poly-cotton is the wrong side of a hard line — it melts onto skin. Past that line the kit is flame-resistant to EN ISO 11612 (with EN ISO 11611 for welding specifically), arc-rated to IEC 61482 for electrical work, and antistatic to EN 1149-5 where flammable atmospheres exist.

The rule that gets missed: FR only works as a system. An FR coverall zipped over a polyester hoodie is a melt layer wrapped in a safe one — mid layers under FR must be FR or natural fibre. And FR garments have their own washing rules; softener and bleach quietly strip the protection.

blocks.h2: The non-safety kit still works for you

items.l: Assembly, QA and stores read as one team — and visitors can find a supervisor
Buy garments rated for the laundry cycle you actually run
Named sets beat communal bins — kit that's yours gets looked after

blocks.html: Boot codes for factory floors (S1P inside, S3 for yard and goods-in) are decoded at the footwear guide; glove markings at the EN 388 decoder.

blocks.h2: Manufacturing kit FAQ

faq.q: What workwear do factory workers need?
faq.a: The common base is a coverall or work trousers with a polo/sweatshirt, S1P safety footwear, and gloves matched to the process — dexterity-first for assembly, cut-rated for sheet metal, nitrile for oily work. Hot works and arc risk move the spec to FR garments under EN ISO 11612/11611 and IEC 61482.

faq.q: Why do machine shops ban loose clothing?
faq.a: Rotating machinery — lathes, drills, mills — catches loose cuffs, drawstrings and untucked hems and pulls the wearer in. Workshop kit is cut snug with closable cuffs for exactly this reason; it's also why gloves are sometimes prohibited at specific rotating machines.

faq.q: Can you wear a normal hoodie under an FR coverall?
faq.a: No — polyester and other melt-prone synthetics under FR defeat the system. In a flash event the FR outer survives while the synthetic mid-layer melts against skin. Under FR, wear FR-rated or natural-fibre layers only.

faq.q: What gloves for handling sheet metal?
faq.a: A cut-resistant coated glove at ISO 13997 cut level C as the starting point, D or higher for heavy, oily or forceful handling. Specify by the letter, not the old coup-test digit — the decoder guide explains the difference.

pages.cardBlurb: Scrubs vs tunics, the 60-degree rule, and kit that survives a 12-hour shift and the laundry that follows.
pages.h1: Healthcare workwear: scrubs, tunics & the 60° rule.
pages.metaTitle: Healthcare & Care Workwear Guide: Scrubs & Tunics | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Workwear for hospitals, clinics and care homes — scrubs vs tunics, laundering at 60°C for infection control, colour-coding by role, and footwear for 12-hour shifts.
pages.lede: Healthcare kit is judged by two audiences at once: the infection-control audit and the person wearing it for twelve hours. The garments that survive both — scrubs, tunics, washable footwear — are chosen on fabric, wash temperature and fit, not looks.

heroMeta.l: The shift the kit must survive

blocks.h2: Scrubs or tunics — it's a workflow question
blocks.html:
Scrubs — loose top and trousers, pocketed, unisex — are the default where clothing changes happen on site and garments cycle through pooled laundry: wards, theatres, dental surgeries, veterinary practice. They're cheap enough to own in numbers and cut for movement.

Tunics — structured, fitted, usually worn with your own trousers — dominate where staff present to the public all day: clinics, care homes, community nursing, salons crossing into aesthetics. They hold their shape through a shift, carry piping or trim for role colour-coding, and read as professional in a way a scrub top doesn't.

Neither is "better" — plenty of employers issue tunics to front-of-house clinical staff and scrubs to everyone behind the doors. The real constants are below: fabric weight, wash survival and fit.

blocks.h2: The laundering facts that decide the fabric

items.l: The common benchmark wash for used healthcare linen and uniforms — the garment must take it, repeatedly
The workhorse blend: survives hot industrial cycles that pure cotton shrinks out of

blocks.h2: Footwear is the forgotten uniform item
blocks.html: Twelve-hour shifts on hard flooring make footwear the item staff care most about — and the one policies say least about. The working spec: washable upper (spills happen), slip-rated sole (an SR mark on safety styles, or dedicated slip-rated occupational shoes where no toe cap is needed), closed toe, and cushioning that survives concrete-under-vinyl. Where portering or stores work involves real impact risk, that's an S2 washable safety shoe rather than a trainer-style clog.

See healthcare kit in a real setting mix at Harrogate — hospitality and care economy. For team embroidery and colour-coding, talk to us before the garments are ordered — colour-coding is easiest to get right up front.

blocks.h2: Healthcare kit FAQ

faq.q: What's the difference between scrubs and tunics?
faq.a: Scrubs are loose two-piece sets built for on-site changing and pooled hot laundering — the wards-and-theatres default. Tunics are structured, fitted garments worn with your own trousers, favoured in care homes and clinics where staff face the public all day and role colour-coding matters.

faq.q: What temperature should healthcare uniforms be washed at?
faq.a: The common benchmark for used healthcare textiles is a 60 °C wash, which is why healthcare garments are cut in poly-cotton blends rated for repeated hot cycles. Follow your employer's uniform and laundering policy — and buy garments that can take it.

faq.q: How many sets of scrubs or tunics do staff need?
faq.a: Enough to change at work and never re-wear between washes — in practice three to five sets per person depending on shift pattern and laundry turnaround. Under-issuing sets is the most common way uniform policies fail in practice.

faq.q: What shoes are best for hospital and care work?
faq.a: Washable uppers, slip-rated soles, closed toes and real cushioning — 12-hour shifts on hard floors are the design brief. Roles with impact risk (porters, stores) step up to an S2 washable safety shoe.

pages.cardBlurb: Why chef whites are engineered, aprons by station, and the front-of-house wardrobe that survives service.
pages.h1: Hospitality workwear: from the pass to the front door.
pages.metaDesc: Kitchen and front-of-house workwear explained — why chef whites are double-breasted cotton, aprons by station, slip-rated footwear, and FOH uniform that survives service.
pages.lede: A kitchen at service is a small industrial site: open flame, hot fat, wet floors, knives. Chef whites look traditional, but every detail is engineering. Front of house has a different brief — look sharp at hour one and hour ten. Here's both wardrobes, done properly.

heroMeta.l: A burn shield you can flip
Wet floors are the top hazard

blocks.h2: Every detail of a chef jacket is doing a job
blocks.html:
The double-breasted front is a reversible splash shield — caught by hot fat, you re-button to the clean, dry layer. The cotton-rich fabric insulates against radiant heat and steam where thin polyester would conduct it (and melt); the knotted or capped buttons survive industrial laundering that shears plastic ones; long sleeves exist for the moment an oven shelf meets a forearm. Modern cuts add vented backs and lighter weaves because 40 °C at the pass is the other occupational hazard.

Below the jacket: chef trousers loose enough to pull away from a scald rather than press it in, and an apron chosen by station rather than habit — that's the table below.

blocks.h2: Aprons by station
head: Station
Apron

rows: Radiant heat and fat spatter — coverage first
Speed and pocket access; splash risk is low
Heavy bib, wipe-clean or leather-front option

Denim or waxed waist apron, branded
Front-of-house visible: part uniform, part protection

blocks.h2: The floor is the kitchen's biggest hazard
blocks.html: More kitchen injuries come from wet, greasy floors than from burns or blades — which makes footwear the highest-value spec on this page. The brief: slip-rated sole (the SR mark under the current standard), closed, liquid-shedding upper against dropped pans and hot spills, and comfort for a double shift on tile. Kitchens with real impact risk — kegs, crates, goods-in — step up to an S2 washable safety shoe: water-resistant upper, toe cap, same slip rating.

items.l: Service marks show on pale poly-cotton by table three — dark, hot-washable fabrics stay presentable
Branded polo or shirt + apron + optional waistcoat flexes from café to fine dining
Logos on FOH kit take hundreds of washes — stitching outlasts print

blocks.html: Chef whites and hygiene laundering in a real town economy: Harrogate. Hot-works clothing in kitchens follows the same fabric logic as industry — the FR washing guide explains why synthetics and heat don't mix.

blocks.h2: Hospitality kit FAQ

faq.q: Why are chef jackets double-breasted?
faq.a: The double front is a working feature: two layers of cotton insulate the chest against heat and splash, and if the outer layer catches hot fat or sauce the jacket re-buttons to present the clean, dry inner layer. It's a burn shield you can flip mid-service.

faq.q: What shoes should kitchen staff wear?
faq.a: Closed, liquid-shedding uppers with a slip-rated (SR) sole and real cushioning — wet, greasy floors cause more kitchen injuries than burns do. Where kegs, crates or goods-in add impact risk, a washable S2 safety shoe adds a toe cap to the same spec.

faq.q: Can chef whites be any colour?
faq.a: Whites are traditional because they show contamination honestly and take boil washing, but blacks and greys are now common front-facing kitchens. The non-negotiables are the fabric and construction — cotton-rich, double-breasted, launderable hot — not the colour.

faq.q: What aprons do different kitchen stations need?
faq.a: Match the apron to the station's hazard: heavyweight full-length cotton for grill and fry, waterproof bibs for pot wash, wipe-clean heavy bibs for prep and butchery, and lighter waist aprons at the pass and front of house where speed and pockets matter more than coverage.

pages.cardBlurb: Multi-norm FR as the base layer, the layering system that keeps it valid, and what offshore adds on top.
pages.h1: Energy & offshore workwear: multi-norm FR done right.
pages.metaTitle: Energy & Offshore Workwear Guide: Multi-Norm FR | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Workwear for energy and offshore — why multi-norm FR coveralls (EN ISO 11612, IEC 61482, EN 1149-5) are the base layer, the FR layering rule, and what offshore work adds.
pages.lede: In most sectors, flame-resistant kit is the exception you reach for. In energy — refineries, gas plants, offshore platforms, major electrical infrastructure — it's the everyday uniform, and the question flips from "do we need FR?" to "which norms, and what goes underneath it?"

blocks.h2: Why energy kit is multi-norm by default
blocks.html:
An energy site rarely presents one hazard at a time — a turnaround crew can face flash-fire risk, arc-flash risk near switchgear and a flammable atmosphere in the same shift. That's why the sector standardised on the multi-norm FR coverall: one garment certified simultaneously to EN ISO 11612 (heat and flame), IEC 61482 (electric arc) and EN 1149-5 (antistatic, for explosive atmospheres), usually with hi-vis to EN ISO 20471 stacked on where vehicles and plant move.

The codes on the label matter individually — 11612 letters A–F grade heat types, 61482 gives an arc class — and the welders' guide unpacks them. What this page adds is the sector's operating rules: the layering system, and what offshore stacks on top.

The layering rule that voids everything else: FR is a system, not a shell. A polyester fleece or synthetic base layer under a certified FR coverall melts in a flash event — inside the garment that just did its job. Under FR, every layer is FR-rated or natural fibre. No exceptions, including the T-shirt.

blocks.h2: Onshore energy vs offshore
blocks.lead: The base is shared; offshore adds marine and survival context on top.
head: Onshore (refinery, gas, grid)
Offshore (platform, vessel)
rows: Multi-norm FR coverall — typically orange, fleet-branded
FR base layers rated for North Sea cold
FR waterproofs; wind is the constant
Arc-rated or cut-rated gloves by task, hard hat
Same, plus grip rated for wet steel
Survival suit for transfers — issued, not bought

blocks.h2: FR kit is a managed asset, not a wardrobe
blocks.html: Multi-norm garments are the most expensive workwear on this site, and they repay management: personal issue with named sets, laundering per the label (softener and bleach strip FR treatments — the wash guide covers it), and retirement on damage, because a torn or contaminated FR garment has lost the protection its price paid for. Hydrocarbon soaking matters specifically: an oil-impregnated coverall can burn regardless of its rating, which is why getting oil out isn't a cosmetic exercise in this sector.

blocks.h2: Three specification habits from the sector

items.l: Specify the exact certifications (11612 codes, 61482 class) — "FR" alone is not a spec
Coveralls are fitted over FR mid-layers, not bare — order accordingly
Badging on FR garments must not compromise the certified fabric — heat-applied transfers need FR-compatible processes

blocks.html: See the sector against a real economy at Aberdeen — offshore, subsea and energy trades. The standards themselves are decoded in the FR & welding guide.

blocks.h2: Energy & offshore kit FAQ

faq.q: What is multi-norm FR workwear?
faq.a: A single garment certified to several protective standards at once — typically EN ISO 11612 (heat and flame), IEC 61482 (electric arc) and EN 1149-5 (antistatic), often with EN ISO 20471 hi-vis. Energy sites standardise on it because their hazards overlap in the same shift.

faq.q: What do you wear under an FR coverall?
faq.a: Only FR-rated or natural-fibre layers — FR base layers, FR mid-layers, cotton. Synthetic fleeces and polyester T-shirts melt in a flash event inside the garment. The layering rule is absolute in this sector, down to the T-shirt.

faq.q: Why is offshore workwear orange?
faq.a: Convention and visibility: orange contrasts against sea, steel and sky, and most operators fleet-brand orange multi-norm coveralls as the platform uniform. It also aligns with the survival and transfer kit ecosystem, which is issued by the operator rather than bought.

faq.q: Does oil contamination really make FR clothing unsafe?
faq.a: Yes — a hydrocarbon-soaked garment can ignite and burn regardless of the fabric's FR rating. Contaminated FR kit comes off shift for proper laundering, and garments that won't come clean are retired. It's a safety rule, not a cleanliness preference.
